title: Manali
selection: Himachal Pradesh recorded 18.0 million domestic and 0.083 million foreign tourist visits in 2024, with foreign visits up 32% (India Tourism Data Compendium 2025). Himachal Pradesh and Manali were existing VacayOut records; this file only fills empty fields, adds new sections and suggests changes to existing ones. v2 (2026-10-28): shared-template pilot — state regions, best time by region and entry points; Manali's areas, transport, fees from the District Kullu permit site, safety, accessibility, common mistakes, FAQs; things-to-do records; 3-, 4- and 7-day plans; 5 travel guides. Not found in any official source: opening hours and entry fees for Hadimba and Manu temples, prices for paragliding, skiing, ropeway and rafting — shown as unconfirmed. Note for the editor: Incredible India's Hidimba page describes three roofs, while its Manali page and Himachal Tourism describe a four-tier structure; the published overview was left unchanged.

overview.text:
Himachal Pradesh is known as 'Dev Bhumi', the land of the gods, for the stone-and-wood temples found in almost every valley. Foreign tourist visits rose 32% in 2024, and the state recorded 18.0 million domestic visits.

In the Kullu valley, Manali is the base for Solang's slopes, the high road over Rohtang Pass and the Atal Tunnel to Lahaul. Down-valley, Naggar Castle has stood since around 1460, and each October Kullu Dussehra brings the valley's deities together at Dhalpur Maidan. The Kalka–Shimla railway is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

best_time.text:
Himachal's seasons differ by region. The lower districts — Bilaspur, Una, Solan, Sirmour, Hamirpur and Kangra — are warm to hot in summer and mild in winter, while Chamba, Kinnaur, Kullu, Shimla and Lahaul-Spiti are mild in summer and cold in winter.

In the monsoon, July and August, roads are slippery and landslides and rock-falls happen, and adventure activities such as rafting and paragliding stop from 15 July to 15 September. High passes have short seasons: heavy snow closes Rohtang Pass in late November and it reopens around May. In Manali, most visitors come from April to July and from October to December.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: five airports serve the state — Chandigarh and Pathankot on its borders, and Gaggal-Kangra, Bhuntar-Kullu and Jubbarhatti-Shimla inside it. Gaggal-Kangra and Pathankot are for Kangra, Dharamshala and Chamba; Bhuntar-Kullu for Kullu-Manali, Mandi and Lahaul-Spiti; Chandigarh and Jubbarhatti for Shimla, Solan and Kinnaur.

By rail: Kalka and Pathankot are the broad-gauge railheads. Narrow-gauge lines climb from Kalka to Shimla — part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site — and from Pathankot through the Kangra valley to Joginder Nagar.

By road: interstate buses run from Delhi, Chandigarh, Jaipur and other nearby cities, and HPTDC runs its own coaches and taxis for sightseeing.

items.title: Is there a train to Himachal?
items.body: Broad-gauge trains reach Kalka and Pathankot. From there, narrow-gauge lines go to Shimla and to Joginder Nagar; everywhere else is by road.

items.title: When is Kullu Dussehra?
items.body: It starts on Vijaya Dashami and runs for seven days at Dhalpur Maidan in Kullu; in 2026 it was held from 21 to 27 October.

overview.text:
Manali, at about 2,050 m in the Beas valley, takes its name from 'Manu-Alaya', the abode of the sage Manu, and is often called the 'Valley of the Gods'. Its best-known shrine is the Hadimba Devi Temple of 1553, in a cedar forest above town; Old Manali has the Manu Temple and relaxed cafés, and Vashisht's hot springs are 3 km away.

Manali is also the region's adventure base: skiing and paragliding at Solang Valley, 13 km away; the Hampta Pass trek; and the high road to Rohtang Pass, 51 km away, which needs a permit. The 9.02-km Atal Tunnel, opened in 2020, runs beneath the pass to Lahaul.

best_time.text:
Manali has two main visitor seasons: April to July, when summer days are around 22–30°C, and October to December. Snow falls mainly from December to early March, and in December–January it can drop below −5°C — the time for skiing at Solang and the Winter Carnival in the first week of January.

The road over Rohtang Pass usually reopens around May and closes in late November; June to August is when visitors drive up to see snow. In the monsoon (July–August) roads can be hit by landslides, and paragliding and rafting stop from 15 July to 15 September. For Solang, Incredible India suggests April to June and September to January.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: Kullu–Manali airport at Bhuntar is 50 km from Manali, with taxis and buses onward. Flights connect it with Delhi (about 1.5 hours), Chandigarh and Shimla.

By bus: Delhi is about 550 km away. Deluxe and AC Volvo buses run regularly from Delhi, Chandigarh, Shimla, Dharamshala and other cities — book ahead. HRTC, HPTDC and private operators run services.

By train: there is no railway to Manali. The nearest railheads are Joginder Nagar, on the narrow-gauge line from Pathankot, and Kiratpur, about 200 km from Kullu on the Chandigarh highway; continue by road.

By car: vehicles not registered in Himachal pay a green tax to enter Manali (₹200 for a car), bought online and valid for seven days.

local_transport.text:
Taxis wait at Manali's local taxi stand. Hire only authorised taxis from registered operators or taxi unions and ask for the government-approved fare chart; HPTDC also runs its own coaches and taxis. HRTC buses leave from the Manali bus stand for major cities.

On foot, Vashisht is linked to the market by a paved path, and the Manu Temple in Old Manali is within walking distance, about 3 km from the main bazaar.

Driving yourself: vehicles not registered in Himachal pay a green tax on entering Manali, and the road to Rohtang Pass needs a separate online permit. Park at the car park near the main market.

where_to_stay.text:
Mall Road and the main market are the most convenient base: the Mall's shops and restaurants are on your doorstep and there is a public car park near the market. Old Manali, up the hill, has narrow lanes and cafés popular with foreign travellers. Vashisht, across the Beas and more compact than Old Manali, has rooftop cafés with mountain views and the hot springs.

Wherever you stay, choose hotels, guest houses or homestays registered with the Department of Tourism.

overview.text: Built in 1553 by Maharaja Bahadur Singh, the Hadimba Devi Temple stands in the Dhungiri cedar forest just above Manali. It honours Hidimba, the wife of Bhima in the Mahabharata, who is worshipped locally as the protector of the valley. The 24-m temple has three square roofs of timber tiles topped by a brass cone. Its carved doorway shows Durga, scenes from Krishna's life and the Navagrahas; inside, a great rock bears the goddess's footprints. A fair is held each May on Hidimba's birthday.

overview.text: Solang Valley, about 13 km from Manali, takes its name from the nearby village of Solang and 'nullah', a stream. It changes with the seasons: in winter its slopes are Manali's ski area, and in summer the meadows fill with paragliders and zorbing. A ropeway climbs above the valley for wide views of the snow peaks. Incredible India suggests April to June and September to January as the best times to visit; for snow, come between December and early March. Nearby, the Atal Tunnel leads on towards Lahaul, while Kothi village and the hot springs of Vashisht make easy stops on the way back to Manali.

places.name: Rohtang Pass

places.seoTitle: Rohtang Pass: Permits, Season & Atal Tunnel

images.alt: A road winding across high grassy slopes towards snow peaks near Rohtang Pass

overview.text:
Rohtang Pass, at 3,978 m on the Pir Panjal range about 51 km from Manali, links the green Kullu valley with the stark landscapes of Lahaul and Spiti. Snow closes the road from about November to May, and the pass is notorious for sudden snowstorms, so check the weather before you set out. Rahala Falls is on the way up.

Since October 2020, the 9.02-km Atal Tunnel has run beneath the pass, connecting Manali with Keylong.

places.seoDescription: Vashisht near Manali: hot springs, bath timings and the temple of Sage Vashisht.

overview.text: Across the Beas, 3 km from Manali and linked to the market by a paved path, the village of Vashisht is known for its sulphurous hot springs and its Kath Kuni-style temple of Sage Vashisht. The baths have a walled stone pool and separate shower rooms for women and men with hot and cold water piped in; charges are nominal, and they are listed as open 7 am–1 pm and 2 pm–9 pm daily. Vashisht is also known for rooftop cafés with mountain views, and a trail leads on to Jogini Waterfall.

images.caption: Naggar Castle

overview.text:
Naggar, about 20 km from Manali, was once the seat of the Kullu kings. Naggar Castle, built around 1460 in the Kath Kuni style of alternating stone and timber, is now a heritage hotel with views over the Beas valley.

The village's temples include the Gauri Shankar Temple, with 12th-century stone carving, and the Tripura Sundari Temple, built of deodar wood. A 30-minute walk from the castle leads to the Nicholas Roerich Art Gallery, with the Urusvati Himalayan Research Institute above it. Incredible India suggests September to November for pleasant weather.

overview.text:
At a walking distance from Manali town, the Manu Temple in Old Manali is a stone-and-wood monument roofed with slate tiles. It is dedicated to the sage Manu, said to have codified Hindu law in the Manusmriti, and it is the only temple in India in his honour.

Legend says that after the great flood Manu first stepped onto the earth here from his celestial boat, and made his home at 'Manu-Alaya' — the abode of Manu, from which Manali takes its name. The temple is about 3 km from the main bazaar, at the top of Old Manali's lanes of cafés.

overview.text:
Jagatsukh, about 6 km from Manali on the left bank of the Beas, was once Nast — the capital of the Kullu rulers for more than ten generations, before the capital moved to Naggar and then to Sultanpur in Kullu. Its old temples include the Gauri Shankar Temple of Shiva and the Gayatri Temple, a reminder of the days when life in the valley centred on the village, and the Chacholi Jatra festival is still celebrated here.

The village can be visited at any time of day, and it is a starting point for treks towards Deo Tibba. It makes an easy stop on the road between Manali and Naggar.

places.seoTitle: Atal Tunnel, Manali: Route, Facts and Tips
places.seoDescription: The Atal Tunnel under Rohtang Pass: 9.02 km long, opened in 2020, cutting Manali to Keylong to 71 km and about 2 hours. Facts and tips for the drive.

images.alt: The portal of the Atal Tunnel set into a snowy mountainside
images.caption: Atal Tunnel

overview.text:
The Atal Tunnel carries National Highway 3 for 9.02 km under the Pir Panjal range, linking Manali with Keylong in Lahaul and bypassing Rohtang Pass. Inaugurated on 3 October 2020, it is the world's longest single-tube highway tunnel above 10,000 ft (3,048 m).

The tunnel changed travel to Lahaul: the old route over Rohtang via Gramphu was 116 km and took 5–6 hours in good conditions; through the tunnel the journey is 71 km and about 2 hours, avoiding stretches prone to avalanches, blockades and traffic jams, especially in winter. Just beyond the north portal, villages such as Sissu have become popular stops.

The season runs from June to September. Vehicles heading towards Hamta need a one-day online pass from the District Kullu permit site. Before you go, tell the local authorities and use only registered guides, porters and licensed agencies.

Bhrigu Lake lies at the base of Bhrigu Peak at about 4,235 m (Himachal Tourism; other sources give about 14,000–14,100 ft). Locals hold it sacred: the sage Bhrigu is said to have meditated beside it.

The lake is about 6 km from Gulaba village on the Rohtang road, and trails start from Gulaba or from Vashisht. Indiahikes rates it a moderate climb past 14,000 ft in four days and runs it from June to September; Incredible India suggests April–June and September–October. Snow falls mainly from December to early March, when temperatures can drop below −5°C. During Manali's Winter Carnival, in the first week of January, a ski competition is held at Solang. overview.text:
The Beas, fed by snow and glaciers on the slopes of Rohtang, runs down the valley from Manali to Kullu, and this stretch is used for white-water rafting, rowing and river crossing. In summer, as the snow melts, the river swells with rapids. Each rafter goes with a qualified instructor who briefs them on safety.

Rules are strict: joy-ride rafting in Himachal is not permitted on rapids above Class II, and rafting stops every monsoon from 15 July to 15 September. Book only with licensed operators, and never climb onto riverside boulders — the river is strong and deceptive. Prices could not be confirmed from an official source.

overview.text:
Rohtang Pass, at 3,978 m and about 51 km from Manali, is the classic day drive for snow. Tourist vehicles need an online permit: ₹500 per vehicle plus a congestion charge at Gulaba bridge (₹50 for cars, ₹100 for buses). Permits are valid for one day, can be applied for up to two days ahead, and are capped at 800 petrol and 400 diesel vehicles a day, released at 10:00 and 16:00; each vehicle can get only three a week. You'll need valid ID, a PUC certificate and a vehicle no older than 10 years, and a printout is compulsory. Fees are not refundable.

On the way up you pass Nehru Kund, Rahala Falls and Gulaba. Heavy snow closes the pass in late November until around May, and June to August is the busiest time. The pass is notorious for sudden snowstorms — check the weather and turn back if it closes in.

overview.text:
Since the Atal Tunnel opened in 2020, Lahaul is an easy day out from Manali. Sissu, a few kilometres beyond the tunnel's north portal, is about 40 km and roughly 1.5 hours from Manali via NH3, and has become a popular stop. The tunnel itself is 9.02 km long; the old road over Rohtang to the same valley was 116 km and took 5–6 hours.

The Sissu panchayat has at times paused tourist activities and stalls by Sissu lake, so check locally before you go. Weather changes fast at this height — carry woollens even in summer.

overview.text:
Kullu Dussehra is Himachal's best-known festival and, unlike Dussehra elsewhere, it begins rather than ends on Vijaya Dashami: it starts that day and continues for seven days at Dhalpur Maidan in Kullu. The celebration opens when the idol of Lord Raghunath, the valley's presiding deity, is pulled on a wooden chariot into Dhalpur ground, and hundreds of village deities arrive with their followers.

In 2026 the International Kullu Dussehra was held from 21 to 27 October, with the Rath Yatra of Lord Raghunath, over 250 hill deities and Nati folk dances. Kullu is 40 km down the valley from Manali and 10 km from Bhuntar airport.

guides.title: Rohtang Pass permit: how it works, fees and rules
guides.summary: Who needs the Rohtang permit, what it costs, when the daily quota opens, the documents you need — and what to do when you can't get one.
guides.seoTitle: Rohtang Pass Permit: Fees, Quota and How to Apply
guides.seoDescription: How the Rohtang Pass permit works: ₹500 fee plus congestion charge, 800 petrol and 400 diesel a day, 10:00 and 16:00 slots, documents and the season.

body.intro: Every tourist vehicle going up to Rohtang Pass needs an online permit from the District Kullu administration. Permits are limited each day, so plan ahead — here is how the system works, using the district's own permit site.

sections.heading: Who needs a permit
sections.text: All vehicles visiting Rohtang Pass for tourism need a permit. It is issued against a daily quota set by the National Green Tribunal and the district, and it is valid for one day only (there and back).

items.title: Permit fee
items.body: ₹500 per vehicle — car, jeep, MUV or bus.

items.title: Congestion charge
items.body: ₹50 for cars, jeeps and MUVs, ₹100 for buses, for crossing Gulaba bridge.

items.title: Refunds
items.body: Fees are not refundable; only failed payments are refunded.

items.title: How far ahead
items.body: Up to two days from the current date.

items.title: Daily quota
items.body: 800 petrol and 400 diesel vehicles a day.

items.title: Time slots
items.body: Released online in two batches: 10:00 and 16:00 (200 diesel and 400 petrol each).

items.title: Weekly limit
items.body: Three permits per vehicle a week (Tuesday to Monday).
Valid ID, a valid PUC (pollution) certificate, and a vehicle registered no more than 10 years ago.
A printout of the permit is compulsory; details must match your documents at the barrier.

sections.heading: Season and weather
sections.text: Heavy snow closes the pass in late November and it reopens around May; June to August is the busiest time. Rohtang is notorious for sudden snowstorms — check the forecast and turn back if it closes in.

sections.heading: If you can't get a permit
sections.text: Drive through the Atal Tunnel instead: 9.02 km under the pass, it reaches Lahaul in about 2 hours and Sissu is about 40 km from Manali. Or spend the day at Solang Valley, 13 km from Manali.

items.title: Green tax
items.body: Vehicles not registered in Himachal pay a separate green tax to enter Manali — ₹200 for a car, valid seven days.

items.title: Special Rohtang permit
items.body: A separate permit issued only once per vehicle per season (60 petrol and 40 diesel vehicles a day).

checklist: Apply online at 10:00 or 16:00, up to two days ahead

body.intro: Manali has no railway and its airport is 50 km away, so most trips from Delhi combine more than one mode. These are the options, with what the Himachal and Kullu district governments say about each.

items.title: Airport
items.body: Kullu–Manali airport at Bhuntar, 50 km from Manali and 10 km from Kullu.

items.title: Flights
items.body: To and from Delhi (about 1.5 hours), Chandigarh and Shimla.

items.title: Onward
items.body: Taxis and buses are available at Bhuntar.

sections.heading: By bus
sections.text: Delhi to Manali is about 550 km by road. Deluxe, semi-deluxe and AC Volvo buses run regularly — Himachal Tourism recommends booking ahead. HRTC, HPTDC and private operators run services, and HRTC buses also link Manali with other major cities.

sections.heading: By train
sections.text: There is no railway to Manali. Take a broad-gauge train to Pathankot and the narrow-gauge line to Joginder Nagar, or a train to Kiratpur, about 200 km from Kullu on the Chandigarh highway — then continue by road.

items.title: Green tax
items.body: Cars not registered in Himachal pay ₹200 to enter Manali, valid seven days; buy online up to nine days ahead and carry a printout.

items.title: Hill driving
items.body: Keep to the left, don't overtake on bends and slow down at corners.

items.title: Monsoon
items.body: In July–August roads are slippery, with landslides and rock-falls.

items.title: Parking
items.body: Use the car park near Manali's main market.

sections.heading: Which to choose
sections.text: Flying is fastest if flights suit your dates; the overnight Volvo is the common budget option; driving gives flexibility for Solang, Rohtang (with a permit) and the Atal Tunnel. Whatever you choose, carry woollens — Manali's weather changes fast.

body.intro: The monsoon changes a Manali trip. Some activities stop by order every year and roads become riskier — but the valley is green and the high treks are in season.

items.title: Adventure ban
items.body: Paragliding, river rafting and river crossing stop every year from 15 July to 15 September.

sections.heading: Roads
sections.text: During the monsoon (July–August) roads are slippery and landslides and rock-falls happen. Drive carefully, keep to the left on hill roads, and build a spare day into your plans.

sections.heading: Rivers
sections.text: The Beas runs high and fast. Don't stand on riverside boulders or cliff edges for photos — Himachal's rivers are strong and highly deceptive.

sections.text: Joy-ride rafting is not permitted above Class II rapids in Himachal, and each rafter goes with a qualified instructor.

sections.text: Tell the SDM, police or tourism office before a high-altitude trek and hire only registered guides and porters. Vehicles heading towards Hamta need a one-day online pass.

sections.heading: Learn properly
sections.text: The Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Mountaineering and Allied Sports in Manali, founded in 1961, runs basic to advanced courses in mountaineering, climbing, trekking, rafting and paragliding.
